speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CANADA-NEW ZEALAND AIR SERVICE REPORTED NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN GREAT BRITAIN AND DOMINIONS AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I desire to direct a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with regard to an associated Press dispatch which appeared the day before yesterday in the Brantford Expositor. The dispatch refers to an announcement made in the British House of Commons by Lieutenant-Colonel A. J. Muirhead, Under-Secretary of State for Air, to the effect that negotiations were under way with the dominions and the United States concerning a proposed air service across the Pacific ocean from Canada to New Zealand.
My question, therefore, is this: Has the Dominion of Canada, as one of the most important dominions concerned in such a proposal, been consulted in regard to this matter, and, if so, does the Prime Minister deem it to

be in the public interest to inform the members of this house as to the present position of the negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADA-NEW ZEALAND AIR SERVICE REPORTED NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN GREAT BRITAIN AND DOMINIONS AND THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The hon. member drew
my attention just before the house assembled to the question he intended to ask; I give him and the house the following information in reply.
The question of an air service across the Pacific ocean between Canada and New Zealand has received informal and preliminary consideration on various occasions. No definite suggestions as to such a service have been put forward, however, and no negotiations are being carried on on the subject at present between the Canadian government and the governments of any other members of the commonwealth.
The statement made by the Under-Secretary of State for Air in the House of Commons at Westminster on May 10 referred not to negotiations on the general subject of the establishment of an air service but to discussions on the preliminary question of the ownership of certain Pacific islands along the proposed route. It is understood that the conversations in question, which are being carried on between the governments of the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand and the government of the United States, are concerned with the ownership of certain islands in the Phoenix group and other islands lying between Honolulu and Australasia.

When the committee adjourned last Friday evening I was calling attention to the cooperation that had existed during the last three years, between the Department of Agriculture of Ontario and the federal department, and I was endeavouring to show that it was not in the best interests of the dairy business, particularly from the standpoint of the marketing of our cheese. I had pointed out that an association known as the Eastern Ontario Dairymen's Association had been in existence for sixty years and had built up the great dairy business of eastern Ontario, from which section the best cheese made in Canada comes, and that their grant of $1,500 had been withdrawn. That grant had been expended entirely on the production end of the business. We knew that if we wished to retain our premium for cheese in the British market we must continue to manufacture a superior quality product, just as I have read in the report which has been submitted that Canada's success in marketing cheese in the United Kingdom depends upon the quality.
I pointed out further that there were two features that marked the success of cheese in Canada; the first was quality and the second, quantity. It was in this direction that the efforts of this association were made. Their grant was withdrawn, however, and the Ontario government permitted an organization known as the Cheese Producers' Association to collect five cents per hundred pounds on all cheese sold in the province. As I said, in 1936 the cheese producers' association collected $22,000, and in 1937 over $38,000, which was supplemented by a grant of $5,000 from the federal department. My contention was that this money was not spent in the best interests of the dairy business. I am not at all opposed to money being spent in the interests of agriculture, but money which, in 51952-1771
my opinion, has been uselessly spent I object to. I have here a copy of the auditor's report of the Cheese Producers' Association of Ontario. New Zealand sent her cheese to Great Britain in consignment. And the cheese was sold in the old country by agents on commission. The Canadian cheese was all sold in Cahada before it left our shores.
This cheese producers' association endeavoured to break up the selling organization, which had been built up in the last seventy-five years, an organization that we were proud of; and I may add that in New Zealand, the leading men there will tell you, they are sorry they ever opened warehouses in Britain and sold cheese as they are doing to-day.
This association of which I am speaking went into the business, borrowing from the banks $204,887.52, with which they purchased cheese. There was appointed in Belleville a man known as a secretary, at a salary of $3,000 and expenses, and he bought the cheese, and another man was sent to London at a salary of $5,000' and expenses and he sold it there. Their auditor's report shows that on their operations they lost $800.82, and the loss would have been considerably more had it not been for the fact that the federal Department of Agriculture came to their assistance and purchased' a large quantity of cheese for shipment to the dried-out area in Saskatchewan for relief purposes. That was the only sale of cheese on which the association made a profit last year.
Let us consider for a moment their other activities-their convention and their office expenses. The auditor's report shows that their receipts come from three sources. The five cents per hundred pounds which the Ontario government allowed them to take-from the farmers on their cheese amounted; to $38,671. Then they received from the county organizations $2,925, and a grant from the federal Department of Agriculture of $5,000, making total receipts of $46,596. Their expenditures included: office and general expenses, $4,308; secretary's salary and expenses,. $4,014. There is a board of five directors who were paid fees amounting to $2,986. A man was sent to England to sell this cheese, and his salary and expenses came to $6,346. Auditing and accounting fees were $625".. Everybody was liberally paid; apparently they," spent all the money they could spend, anct wound up the year with a surplus of $18,935, which they did not know what to do with. Yet they had taken from the farmers who- sent milk to the cheese factories $38,671 and had received a grant from this government of $5,000. I know that their secretary has gone back to London. A friend of mine told me

Supply-Agriculture-M arketing
he met him on the street there a couple of weeks ago and asked him what he was doing there, and he said, " I came here in the interest of the Ontario Cheese Producers' Association." Some of this nearly $19,000 that they had left is being spent in that way. My contention is that not one dollar of that money was of any benefit to the dairymen. Every report of the dairy business with the old country has shown, and those of us who have spent our lifetime in this business know, that the success of our cheese in the old country depends first on quality and then on the quantity that we can supply. Our money should be spent on the production end, and not foolishly wasted in the selling end.
What year is that report for?

The auditor's report for 'the year ended December 31, 1937. During the three years that this cooperation has been going on and that attention has been diverted from the production end and directed towards the selling end, what has happened to our cheese? I receive every week during the production season a statement from the dairy and cold storage branch of the Department of Agriculture giving the prices of New Zealand cheese in England and the cable prices in Canada. It had been always known that Canadian cheese sold at a premium over New Zealand cheese. I have here some figures taken from the returns given to me by the Department of Agriculture. I find that in 1934 there was a premium of 3 to 4 shillings per hundredweight of 112 pounds for Canadian cheese over New Zealand. But in 1937 we find this reversed: in July and August of that year there was a premium of 3 to 5 shillings per hundredweight in favour of New Zealand.
I know that figures have been produced and statements made at some of our public meetings by officials of the department to show that Canadian cheese was at a premium over New Zealand cheese. But how did they arrive at it? New cheese is selling in Canada to-day for about 15 cents a pound wholesale, but go into any grocery store and ask for old matured cheese and you will have to pay 30 to 35 cents. Would it be fair for me to come to this committee and say that that is the price of cheese? Not at all. Yet the grocers' price has been taken in London to show that we still have a premium, and that price included the old cheese. It is a well known fact that New Zealand manufactures a very moist cheese, which is palatable when it is fresh but has no keeping quality. Invariably the British merchant buys Canadian cheese when he wants to have old cheese.

I have looked over the new report which came to my hand to-day. It says:
Canada has two important advantages over competing countries in having almost to the complete exclusion of competing countries, the trade in mature cheese for the retail trade and for the manufacture of pasteurized processed cheese. There is little doubt that with continued attention to quality Canadian producers can retain these advantages.
We have to the almost entire exclusion of other countries the market for old matured cheese, and it can be retained if we keep up the quality of our product. A report which I got from the department showed that for the last three years the premium upon cheese had dropped. In 1935 it was cents; in 1936, it was cents and in 1937, one cent. But that included the old matured cheese. The figures I have given are taken from the report of the department, giving the wholesale prices. My contention is that this money has been spent on the selling end where nothing could be accomplished, and that the production end, where everything can be accomplished in regard to both quality and quantity, has been neglected. I want to read a statement from the report of the chief grader. He said:
The total cheese placed below first grade last season was 94,546 boxes, an increase of 39,792 boxes over the previous year. The total loss on these cheese was approximately $90,000 and the extra loss owing to an increased percentage of under-grade cheese was about $38,000. This is a tremendous loss to the cheese industry, but I do not imagine that the larger quantity of under-grade cheese would affect the reputation of Canadian cheese on the markets of the United Kingdom if our first grade cheese was equal to the standard of quality for previous years.
Even our first quality cheese was not up to the standard.
I have no definite information on this point which would apply to the season's make. However some reports have come back that July and August cheese were not quite up to former years, and we also know that there were many shipments of first grade cheese on which the total score was lower than 92 points owing to slight defects in workmanship.
Then let me read another clause from the report of the chief grader. Referring to a chart which is shown he says:
This chart shows the grading of Ontario cheese throughout each month of the season and this indicates that there was a decrease in first grade every month excepting May. Weather conditions should be very favourable during the latter part of September, also in October and November, but decreases in the percentage of first grade are shown during these months, and the inference, therefore, would be that even with good weather conditions either the milk producers or the cheese makers or perhaps both, were not doing their job as well as it should be done.

Supply-A griculture-M arketing
Here is the point: We have been allowing the quality and to some extent the quantity of our cheese, the only things over which we had any control, to be neglected. What did that mean to the farmers? Last year nearly 839,000 was forcibly taken from the pockets of the farmers by an assessment made on their cheese at the factories, and in addition, with the cuts that were made on low grade cheese, in the selling end they lost 8128,000. That is taken from the report of the chief grader. I am not at all opposed to money being spent if the dairy industry, or any other branch of agriculture, is getting the benefit of it, but in the last quarter century we have had only one minister of agriculture in this house who seemed to understand the dairy business and the intricacies of mixed farming in eastern Canada. That minister was the present hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell). I have been connected with this business all my life, and during the term of office of the hon. gentleman I discussed these matters with him on many occasions. He was born and brought up in the county in which I live; his home was outside the town of Perth, and he lived there until he was twenty-one years of age. He was brought up on a dairy farm; he understood the requirements of our great dairy business.
I would simply ask the minister this, that in future he see to it that the money voted is spent where it will bring some benefit to the farmers engaged in the business. I am not asking him not to vote the money, but simply to see that some good results from it.
I do not think I need argue this matter further at this time. My whole intention has been to lay before the minister and the committee the necessity of seeing that the money is properly expended, for the purpose for which it is intended, and I claim that not one dollar of this money brought any benefit whatever to the dairy industry. It is utterly impossible for a few men to think they can buy a few cheeses, ship them over to . London and break up a selling organization that has existed in this country for the last seventy years, and of which we are justly proud. As a result of the efforts of these few gentlemen to whom I have referred they lost 8800 last year, without taking into consideration the salaries and expenses of the men who were doing the work. They lost on the actual buying and selling of the cheese, so I would ask the minister in future to maintain more strict supervision over the expenditure of these amounts.

I am rather at a disadvantage, Mr. Chairman; I came into the house
while the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) was speaking, and certainly I was unaware that there was to be a speech of this kind dealing with this question. I realize that the riding represented by the hon. member for Lanark is more interested in the question of cheese than the riding which I represent. We do a good deal of dairying in Renfrew county, but principally in connection with the manufacture of butter rather than cheese.
Because I was not aware that this question was coming up I have none of the figures before me, but I must take very strong exception to the view that has been expressed by the hon. member for Lanark. Particularly must I take exception to an hon. member of this house adopting the attitude that the farmers of Canada ought not to bother their heads about the marketing of their own products. If there is one thing the farmers of this dominion ought to learn it is to pay some attention to the marketing of their products. We have been given, not only by the Department of Agriculture but by the farmers' organizations themselves, a great deal of education with regard to the proper grading of our products. During the past few years we have learned to sell our eggs on a graded basis. We have learned to a certain extent the proper type of hog to produce for the British market. We are learning that we ought to have our cream in proper condition so that we may produce the proper quality of butter for our markets. All this sort of education has been of great benefit not only to the producers but also to the consumers throughout Canada. Now we have reached a stage in the cheese industry, as far as grade is concerned, where there is not very much opportunity for improvement. Something happened last year, of course, that caused our grade to go down to some extent, but two years ago, if I remember correctly, our cheese graded something like ninety-eight per cent No. 1.
Here we have an effort on the part of the farmers of Ontario to get together in an organization of their own, financed by themselves, receiving a small grant from the federal treasury, and to improve the marketing of this important product. We must remember that in regard to cheese we are almost entirely dependent upon the export market. Our home market is very limited; we do not appear to be a cheese eating people. The situation is very different in regard to butter; we consume practically our total production of butter, but we must sell our cheese in outside markets. Here we have farmers representing every county in which cheese is manu-

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
factured. These men get together and form an organization, which is surely a democratic organization, with directors appointed for each county. These men get together to-study the whole question, and they make an -effort to improve matters in connection with the selling of this product, to my mind with very considerable success as a beginning. It is true that they had a man in England last year, and I believe that this feature of their work is not being carried on this year. Even at that they are experimenting and studying the whole question. Yet we have the spectacle of a member of this house who represents a dairying section of the country objecting to farmers getting together and doing something for themselves in connection with the sale of their own product.
I submit that the farmers are entirely within their rights when they get together and say, "We are going to impose the small tax of one-tenth of a cent per pound, or five cents per hundred pounds, in order to make our contribution towards the organization." We must remember that that organization is in its infancy. They are experimenting and trying to find out how they can improve the market for and the sale of their own product. Yet this hon. member who comes from a farming community objects, contending that the farmers ought to attend to the production end and leave the selling to somebody else. That "somebody else" would mean commission houses; certainly they will take care of their own profits. The farmers, I repeat, are entirely within their rights in making an effort along these lines in order to better the selling of their product. If the Department of Agriculture is willing to give assistance to the organization by way of a small grant I am sure such assistance would be appreciated by the farmers of the province.
I have discussed the work of the organization with the heads of the Department of Agriculture and I find they are in complete accord with what is being done. They believe the efforts of the organization will be of considerable value to the farmers. I am entirely in favour of farmers getting together at any time to improve the marketing of their own products, and certainly to my mind there should be no objection when they are willing to finance the scheme by imposing a small tax on themselves.

Before the discussion proceeds further may I point out that we are *discussing item No. 8, but it is item No. 6 that is before the committee. If hon. members are prepared to pass item 6 and proceed
(Mr. Warren.J
to discuss No. 8, I shall be content. I do suggest however we should discuss the items as they come before the committee.
Under what item may we discuss matters in connection with beef cattle?
Item No. 11.

When the item was before the committee the other evening there was some discussion about what is commonly known as the Shaw report. The minister stated frankly that the report had been somewhat changed.
I am pleased to state that to-day I received by mail a copy of the new edition

I do not know whether I should call it a report, because it is not so designated.
I believe the old report was concurred in by all the members of the committee who went overseas. I stated the other evening that some very good men were on that committee. Certainly the officials of the department who visited England are efficient and capable men.
I have no reason to believe that they would include in a report statements with which they are not fully in accord. In fact the initial report in its foreword, signed by the director of marketing services, Mr. Shaw, states that the findings and recommendations contained in the report are agreed to in principle by all members of the party. Yet we find that shortly after the report was printed and issued it was suppressed and distribution cancelled; meantime a new report has been drafted and is now presented to parliament. In many respects the new report is different from the old one. The other evening I asked the minister why the changes had occurred, and he replied they bad been made because of certain complaints and because of certain reports which had been issued; I cannot think however that those were all the reasons for the change. I feel that complaints have been made from certain quarters of which we have not been made aware.
I asked the minister if any of the industries or interests connected with the marketing of farm products had objected, and he said they had not. But there is undoubtedly some reason, and a very important one. for the change in and the redrafting of the report and for the incorporation in the new report of matters which were not in the old one.
It seems to me that to change a report drafted by a committee which spent a considerable sum of money in connection with the matter is an unusual procedure. The report has been garbled, certain of the findings have been left out, and some of the recommendations have been changed. I suggest the minister should make a more frank state-

Supply-A gricul ture-M arke ting
ment than he made the other evening as to what occurred, why the report was changed and from what points the complaints came. He should take the committee into his confidence, because I believe if he does so he may hasten the passage of this particular item.
May I point out to the minister that I was discussing the marketing end of the matter, and would appear to have been in order.
Item No. 8 is the item with respect to dairy products. Marketing services in connection with dairying products would come under item No. 8. We are discussing administration at this time.
I wanted an opportunity to reply to the hon. member for Renfrew North.
We will come back to that subject, but at the present time I should like to have the discussion in proper order. If we are going to run up and down the list we will be in difficulty all the time.
All right.

The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has raised a matter which was discussed the other evening. I believe he has very effectively in his first few observations answered the question which is in his mind. He pointed out that the first pamphlet issued was the report of a committee. As I indicated the other night that was a committee composed of some officials of the department, and some officials of farmers' organizations and of one canning organization, all outside the department. Those men went to England and examined into the conditions surrounding the marketing of farm products in Great Britain, and in pursuance of their observations made a report. I believe it goes without saying that a committee of that kind writing a report would be likely to make some recommendations which any government in office would find it impossible to put into effect. They might even make some criticism of the activities of the government of the day. However, they would make their report on the basis of what they themselves considered to be fair in connection with the case.
A report of that kind was issued and, as was stated a few moments ago, it was published. Somewhere between five and six thousand copies in English and French were printed and in the neighbourhood of 5,000 copies were circulated throughout Canada. I believe every hon. member of this house received a copy, as well as the members of most of the legislatures of the different provinces; each daily
newspaper in Canada received a copy as well as all the agricultural papers. I believe that most of the farm organizations of one kind or another also received copies. In other words, there was a wide distribution of the publication.
The statement I made the other evening was that after the press summary had been handed out there was one statement which perhaps unduly called attention to certain findings of the committee and made it appear that those would likely be acted upon. As a result of criticisms that were made, the report was not circulated to the general public but it was left in the possession of the press. It was not suppressed; as a matter of fact it was placed in the hands of every publicity organization in this country. Most of the newspapers across Canada wrote editorials having to do with the report or commented upon it in one way or another. I venture to say that no report made by a committee to any department of government has had more publicity than the one we are now discussing.
The department decided, and I as minister take responsibility for that decision, that an outline of the policies adopted as a result of this report and certain information which the report contained, would be more beneficial to the general public, particularly to the farmers throughout Canada, as indicating the ways and means that were going to be adopted, than the report itself. I asked that the publication which would go out to the general public as a result of requests coming in should contain the actual policy of the department, decided upon after having had the report of the committee. What I read the other evening was the main part of the new pamphlet that was brought out and which sets forth the policy of the government decided upon as a result of having obtained the report of -this committee, presented to us I believe on December 8 last. In the first division of this new publication on- pages 8, 9 and 10, will be found set out the general policy, and the pages following will be found to contain the information gathered by the committee that it was considered would be of general interest to the people of Canada. These pages contain the information that they should have to arrive at conclusions as to what might be done, either by processing organizations or the producers themselves, to produce a product up to the standard and grade that is intended to be handled through the department.
I think these explanations cover everything that has happened up to date. If there are

In common with many other publications got out by the department, it contains information with regard to the policies of the government in connection with marketing. It contains information on marketing gathered by the committee.

The previous one was a report.

This seems to me to be a strange procedure. I agree with the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) when he says that there should be more explanation by the minister as to why this change was made. I have not a copy of the old report before me, but I have one of the new. I hope it is not because of conflict between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture. There has been danger of that under other governments as well as under this one, and I believe it has not been eliminated entirely at the present time. As the old saying is, " the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life," and as we are all interested in marketing conditions overseas, the wording of this very important document may mean very little. I commend the government for any efforts they have made and for any they propose to make in the future in connection with investigating conditions overseas. For many years I have felt that our governments have been all too lax in making thorough investigations into the needs of the consumers in this and other countries. This information is essential to a country that depends upon export markets for the disposal of a considerable proportion of its agricultural products. It seems to be even more important to our domestic welfare in this country in view of the fact that we consume in our own markets the greater percentage of what we produce. Fortunately perhaps at times, but at many times unfortunately, a small surplus automatically sets the price at home. It is therefore most essential that our markets overseas should be carefully studied and every assistance given in order not only to standardize products but to classify our exports and regulate the supply so that a fair price may be maintained.

This committee made a careful study of the publicity used by those countries to advertise their products and the policies followed in order to regulate their supplies and standardize their grades; and, strange as it may seem, the table of contents shows that the publicity and policies of the exporting countries of Australia, New Zealand, the Union of South Africa and even Canada are left out entirely.

I believe we need better marketing conditions overseas, and I further believe that only by careful study-of the requirements can we lay sound and reasonable plans for supplying those markets. I feel that we have made too little study of these problems in the past. I do not propose to continue at any great length, Mr. Chairman, except to submit once more that the marketing of our agricultural products is seriously affected by the importation into this country of enormous quantities of the same products we are trying to sell. When we realize that enormous quantities of vegetable oils and vegetable fats which could be replaced with animal fat within our own borders are coming into this country; that we are now trying to find a market for over half of the lard produced in Canada, and that each year fifty train loads of vegetable oils come into Canada duty free, half of which consists of edible vegetable . oils and replaces animal fats and lard used for cooking purposes we must understand that if that procedure is not stopped it will soon destroy the live stock industry of Canada. I make that statement as a farmer.
In his responsible position as a member of the government I believe the Minister of Agriculture, even though he may have clung to other fiscal theories in the past in connection with the marketing of agricultural products, should talk the matter over with the Minister of Finance. I well recall that when the Minister of Finance entered the house he showed strong inclinations towards

that old and dusty doctrine of free trade. But the longer he sat in the house and the longer he has faced the problem the more he has realized that if we are going to develop Canadian resources we must bury the old differences between our fiscal policies and realize that in the marketing of the products of agriculture we are confronted with the competition of cheaply produced agricultural substitutes of other countries, and that those substitutes have been just as disastrous and have just as effectively hindered the farmers of Canada as have the longer working hours, lower wages and lower standards of living hindered the manufacturing industry.
I have always stated and repeat to-day that the farmers of Canada are entitled to the same fiscal policy as the industrialists. There must not be one policy for one class and another for another. I do not suggest for a moment that because we have millions of pounds of oil entering Canada and taking the place of our own product the government should make a political gesture and state that in lieu thereof it will take the duty off farm implements, or something of the kind. The farmers of Canada do not wish to destroy another man's opportunity for employment. But they are concerned with the fact, as is every other citizen, that there must be jobs for their boys, jobs for their neighbours' boys, and markets for their products not only overseas but at home. Ninety-five per cent of the live stock produced in Canada is marketed at home. The committee was well advised on that point when it considered the marketing and publicity policies of Australia and New Zealand. We find that these countries consume only about fourteen per cent of their agricultural products, and must find an export market. The export market is almost their only market. But in Canada we have a vastly different condition; the development has been the other way. Our great market for agricultural products is right here in Canada. We realize that more fully when we are told that twelve carloads of meat go to Kirkland Lake every week. The district surrounding Timmins, and other extensive mining sections, provide important markets which must be given careful consideration.
I agree with many of the recommendations which have been made, and I hope the government may see fit to put them into effect. I believe there should be a national market. I believe the committee said there should be an empire market; the second edition however does not say that.

That might be well justified. I submit in all seriousness that the government should give consideration not particularly to licensing exporters, but that they may more carefully guard their products. To-day in Canada three-quarters of a million families are affected by the prosperity of agriculture. In view of the small amount of agricultural products exported from Canada I believe the government might be well advised to consider the advisability of a bonus policy in connection with the export of high class agricultural products.
All one needs to do is to drive along the roads of Canada and to see the buildings in need of repair in the rural districts to know that the standard of living in those districts is not comparable to that of even the humblest urban resident. Improvement along this line would involve an enormous amount of employment in Canada and an enormous amount of business.
I realize that while only a small portion of our agricultural production is exported, it is that small amount which sets the price in the home market. Someone may ask, "What about the consumers' league?" I would say, and I have no doubt the hon. member for Huron North would agree, that the consumers are not so much concerned about what they have to pay for their food, if they receive reasonable wages.
What about the housewives in Toronto?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, May 11, consideration in committee of Bill No. 52, respecting radio in Canada-Mr. Howe- Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 5,-Station licences.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
When this bill was last discussed I was answering a suggestion by the hon, member for York South (Mr. Lawson) that there had been some deception in the explanatory notes of the bill; that the evidence of this was in clause 5, and that the real purpose of the clause was to take care of radios in automobiles. As a matter of fact, the old Radiotelegraph Act amply covered automobiles. It provided that a licence fee was collectable for a radiotelegraph station anywhere; and, of course, under the old act a radio receiving set is a radiotelegraph station. One statement my hon. friend made and strongly emphasized was that radios in automobiles were unknown in 1913. Just to dispose of that assertion, I have before me the year book of wireless telegraphy and telephony, 1913, and in it we have a photograph of a motor car wireless telegraph station which I should be glad to send across to my hon. friend simply to show him that wireless in automobiles was not unknown in 1913, as he so dogmatically stated. However, the purpose of the change in the article other than the change in the phraseology is to take care of the flaw in the previous legislation which was brought out in the Gignac case, in which the judge found that use of a radio must be proved by actual evidence of use; that is, the inspector must find, to prove use, the owner of the radio actually with the power turned on and turning the dial. In the Gignac case the defendant was convicted of installing a radio without a licence; but it was quite clear from the finding of the judge that had the installation taken place before the time limit-I think it is one year-in which complaint must be made, he could not have been- convicted on a charge of illegal installation. Section 5 in its present wording is inserted to close the opening left by the decision in the Gignac case, and the provision for exemption of visiting automobiles is simply put there to
provide for a situation which was not provided for in the old act. Under the old act a radio in a visiting car was taxable, and this makes it clear that there will be an exemption.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I cannot help remarking that the minister had to go a long way to find this ancient vintage of an automobile which was apparently equipped with a radio.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: My hon. friend said it was unheard of in those days.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I think the committee understood what I meant, that it was unheard of in any passenger vehicle used by people to run about the country. I observe, in the very fine photograph sent me by the minister, that attached to the rear of this so-called automobile are about eighteen telephone poles. I assume those were to carry the station, and I would draw to the minister's attention that if he had but read the article which goes with the picture he would have found that this was not an ordinary case of a radio being installed in a pleasure motor car, but one of a motor car being built purposely to have a radio station which, by reason of being moved about from place to place, changed the wave length and thereby preserved secrecy for signals which were then being transmitted by radio.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I am wondering if this section 5 makes it necessary for a person to pay an extra licence fee if he has in his possession an obsolete radio. If one is keeping as an heirloom a radio presented to him in years gone by, is it going to be necessary for him to pay a licence fee every year? I notice it says:
No person shall . . . have in his possession any radio apparatus.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: That is right. It is necessary to have it.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
What is the answer to
the question?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: If a man had two radios, would he have to pay two licence fees if the radios were in the same house?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Yes, and if the radio apparatus is in the man's house the onus of proof is on the owner to show it is not in use. Under this legislation possession is presumption of use.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
There is a question which I wish to ask the minister and which, I believe, was asked in the committee, and Major Murray said he would get a ruling on it. A man lived in a town in which there were electrical facilities; his house was

Radio Broadcasting
wired, but he was not using the electricity for any purpose, and he had given to him a battery set. The question arose, Would he have to have a licence for a battery set or an electrical set, if he was in a town in which electrical facilities were provided but was not using them in any way in his house?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: We obtained a ruling on that point from the Department of Justice. The department ruled that if a house is not connected with the electric current the owner would pay a battery set licence fee.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: But whether it was wired or not, if he was not using the electricity for any purpose?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: There, again, it would depend upon whether the owner could prove be was not using the electricity in the house. If the electric wiring was installed the onus of proof would be on the owner to show he was not using electricity in his house.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: The man who wrote to me stated that when he moved into the house he did not figure he could afford electricity, so he had the meter turned off. The house was wired, because the people who occupied the house before him had been using electric lights and electricity. When he came in he had the meter shut off and did not use electricity, and he had a battery set given to him. The question is whether he had to pay $2.50 or $2 for his licence. I maintain that as he was using a battery set and was not using electricity for any purpose he should not be required to pay $2.50 for that battery set. That is the question on which we wanted a ruling.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: The case is, I should say, most unusual. I should say he was quite justified in taking out a battery set licence, but to make absolutely sure of the law it might ibe well to advise him to disconnect the wiring into his house.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: That would be entirely up to the man who owned the house, not to the renter.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Would the minister point out where in this legislation one is exempt from committing an offence under it if he merely has in his possession a radio, and it is not in use. In answer to a question by one of my hon. friends to my left, the minister said the onus is on the accused to show that the set is not in use, and left the inference that if it were not in use then it was not an
offence under the legislation to have it. I am sorry, but that is not the way in which I read the bill. The section says:
No person shall establish any radio station or private receiving station, or install, operate or have in his possession any radio apparatus. . . .
Apparently merely having it in one's possession is an offence, unless the minister can show me where, somewhere else in the bill, the non-user exempts one from the offence prescribed by section 5.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Perhaps I can explain the point this way. Complaint comes to the department in various ways that there is an apparatus in a house. Before any prosecution takes place a permanent officer of the department visits the house. If it can be proven to him that this apparatus is not in use, no prosecution follows. Provision in the law in that connection brings up the old question involved in the Gignac case, that we must prove use. To prove use you must see the apparatus in use. Two witnesses must see it being used, the current turned on and the dials being manipulated. That is the ruling in the Gignac case. Having a radio apparatus in your possession is covered by the legislation, but in the operation of it our officer is instructed to make very sure that the apparatus is usable. To define that in the bill, however, would lead us into the same technical difficulties that were encountered under the old act.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
In other words, the question whether I am to be prosecuted or not for having in my possession a radio is one which is to be decided at the will of a civil servant of the Dominion of Canada, and frankly I object to being put into that position. I object not only on my own behalf, but also on behalf of the people of Canada who may be subjected to prosecution. Furthermore, I think the minister is badly advised when he says that provision could not be made for the situation which I have mentioned without going right back to the position that prevented conviction in the case of Rex v. Gignac. By a clause of this bill the onus is put on the accused. The moment a person is accused of an offence, the onus is put on him of proving that he is not guilty, and that being so, the accused, once he is charged, must satisfy the court that he is not guilty. The reason that the crown lost in the Gignac case was that the onus was on the prosecution of establishing that the machine had been installed or had been operated, and the crown could do neither. That, however, will no longer prevail. Now, a man can be haled into court for mere
Radio Broadcasting

possession, and the onus is on him to establish non-user. Surely, under these circumstances, a clause could be inserted in the bill providing that where an accused satisfies the court that the radio apparatus was not in use in the licence year in which he was prosecuted, there should be no offence under section 5. That, it seems to me, can be set out without in any way weakening the legislation or embarrassing its enforcement.
If that cannot 'be done, we come back to the general objection that I made in connection with this bill. In my opinion, it is a great mistake in our legislatures, whether it be the House of Commons, or a provincial house, to give some particular body, whether civil servants or other individuals, any one you like, the power to determine whether or not I have committed an offence or whether I should be prosecuted. That power should be given only to those who are duly appointed and constituted judicial officers. In reading current reports in the press I find that I am not alone in that view. Before coming into the house to-night I noticed a statement in the press that the attorney general of Ontario, an attorney general, by the way, of a Liberal administration, agrees entirely with that view and says that he is unalterably opposed to this legislation.
I suggest to the minister that he confer with the Minister of Justice as to the wisdom of this legislation leaving discretionary power in the hands of any civil servant to determine who shall or shall not be prosecuted; for when he determines the question of prosecution he likewise determines the question of guilt or innocence, because under the section as it now stands the mere possession of a radio apparatus constitutes an offence.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: This section was drawn up by the officers of the Department of Justice in the light of the Gignac case, but I shall be glad to allow the section to stand and ask the Minister of Justice to review the situation having regard to what my hon. friend has said, and I must say that I have some sympathy with his point of view. We shall see if a workable clause can 'be drawn along the lines he suggests.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: While the clause is being redrafted, some provision ought to be made to enable dealers to have radio sets in their possession without having to obtain licences. I cannot see how they can do that under this clause as it now stands, but perhaps I misinterpret it.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
The situation with regard
to dealers is taken care of in the regulations. No special legislation is required.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Perhaps I am saying what has already been said; but it seems to me that the principle of putting on the accused the onus of establishing his innocence is altogether contrary to fundamental principle of British procedure, whereby a man is considered innocent until he is proved guilty. I greatly object to having that principle violated just for the sake of S2.50. It is offensive to me to see a man put in the position where he might be declared a criminal and made a gaolbird in consequence of a law of this sort.
Section stands.
Section 6 agreed to.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

On section 9-Search warrant.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Again I am going to ask the minister to consider seriously the wisdom of this section. I realize that with two exceptions it is not vastly different from the old section 11 which was in the act passed in 1913. Under the act of 1913 a search warrant could be issued only by a magistrate to a duly constituted police officer within his jurisdiction, whereas under this section it may be issued to one of many persons therein indicated. Furthermore, under the old section it could not be issued on the mere allegation of possession of a radio set. I would point out that the old Radiotelegraph Act was passed in 1913, and despite the picture in the book of an automobile which had a radio in it, it never was conceived that the act was directed against the ordinary citizen

Radio Broadcasting
who had a radio set in his home. In those days radio, as far as commercial use was concerned, was confined to ships at sea and to land stations that communicated from land to land or land to ship. In such circumstances it was necessary, where illegal stations were established, without licence, that a search warrant should be issued on the allegation that there was such an illegal station established, because the lives of passengers on ships at sea might be endangered by it, or international complications might arise from messages falsely transmitted by such illegal stations from one country or nation to another. In that situation and under those circumstances these drastic clauses were necessary. But let us bear in mind that all the business of radio stations in respect of ships, etc., has now been taken out of this legislation.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Just in respect of ships.
_ Mr. LAWSON: All right; all radio stations in ships have been taken out of this legislation and transferred to the shipping act. Surely it is not the minister's intention that these drastic powers should be given in respect of entering people's homes. I do not want to take the time to run over all the arguments that one reads in newspapers and that have been advanced as to the opportunities it would give for crooks to gain entry to people's homes and that sort of thing. Suffice it to say that under this bill a land station, that being, I assume, a commercial radio station is defined, and a private receiving station is also defined. Private receiving stations are in people's homes. If it is necessary to pass any legislation as drastic as that contained in section 9 and two others to which I shall refer later, confine it to your land stations; do not let us extend these arbitrary and unreasonable powers of entering people's homes in order to deal with some man who may have committed the very minor offence of having in operation a radio for which he has not paid S2.50 for a licence.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I assume it is the intention of the legislation to collect 82.50 from every user of a radio. There is no change in the intent of this section. If my hon. friend will look at the old act he will find it has exactly the same provision. Since 1932 it has been the custom to have warrants to enter homes in order to obtain evidence for prosecution. When I came into this office I tried to avoid that situation, naturally everyone who has had to do with this, even as a private citizen, knows the present system is very objectionable. We tried to find some alternative, but we found our collections of radio licences would
drop by half, were it not for the ability to obtain evidence to prosecute. It is only the fear of prosecution that holds the collection of radio licences up to where it is to-day, and it is far from 100 per cent to-day. If any other workable plan can be found I would be glad to adopt it. Collection of radio licence fees by present methods is most difficult. It causes more complaint and upset than anything else in the department. But after two years of diligent search we have found no other practical way of collecting this fee, without an expenditure out of proportion to the amount to be collected.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: There are thousands of things for which a licence fee is imposed, municipal, provincial and dominion; but no one in his senses would conceive of giving the right to enter a man's home and search, in order to collect it. Let me take a couple of examples that occur to me at the moment. In the municipality in which I live, and, I think, in every other municipality, you must have a licence to keep a dog. Would not any parliament be laughed to scorn that would pass legislation authorizing a warrant to search a man's home in order to ascertain whether he has a dog?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: A radio does not go out walking like a dog.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Where I live you are not allowed to let a dog off your premises or be at large. Dogs can be kept in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: But they may be taken out on a leash.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
That is true, but if the minister persists in this legislation I am afraid he may be taken out on a leash by the public before he is finished.
There are dozens of things for which one requires a licence, but parliaments do not give authority to issue search warrants to go into people's houses and search for such things. The minister says this is necessary if licence fees are to be collected. I do not think that is quite true. I admit that when it was necessary for the crown, in order to get a conviction for failure to have a licence, to prove that the person charged had either actually installed a radio or actually operated it, such powers might be required. But that is not going to be so in future. By this bill you are making it an offence for a man merely to be in possession of a radio. If he is in possession, the onus is on him to show that he was not operating it. All any police officer has to do is to peek through the window and he can see whether there is a radio on the floor
Radio Broadcasting

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Is that a legal act, to peek through a window?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: It is a legal act for a police officer.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Not a very dignified one.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Unquestionably not. But, in fact, it is not an illegal act even for ordinary individuals, except under certain circumstances which I shall not at the moment describe. But in all seriousness, when you have made it an offence merely to have possession of a radio-

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Oh, I presume you are. I never dreamed that you would think of changing. That is why I asked the minister to reconsider the section. After all, it is not a matter of life and death to this country if we fail to collect two or three per cent of all the radio licences.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Or fifty per cent?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Fifty per cent is a very different matter, but with the amended legislation contained in this bill you have at your disposal the means of collecting ninety-five per cent of the radio licences without exercising the right to search a man's home. I want to say to the minister in all seriousness-

speechtext:
I just want to say to the minister that we should not lose sight of this

fact, and I am not making this allegation against this government in particular. There is a terrible tendency in legislatures and parliaments in general in this country to-day to go on curtailing and interfering with what we have always regarded as the inherent right of a British subject, namely that his home is his castle. I for one will not allow these fundamental principles of rights to be interfered with lightly, and though I realize-

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS

speechtext: I think it could be obtained in many ways. For example, a radio inspector calls at my house. He asks if I have a radio licence, and I say no; then he asks me if I have a radio. Ninety-nine per cent of the people will answer yes or no.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: There are not many who are wise enough to say, "Mind your own business," and shut the door in his face.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: A very large percentage say exactly that.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
All right, then; if a very large percentage say exactly that, nothing could be a clearer indication of the feeling of the people of this country in connection with this whole business of radio licences. I would ask the minister to bear in mind that neither this nor any other government on earth can maintain and enforce a law which has not behind it the great weight of public opinion, I do not care what your law may be.
To come back to the question, I suggest that your inspector or police officer, by looking in the window of a house, could see if there was a radio in that house. I suggest also that, for example, you get a record of every radio which is sold in Canada. I could

go down to the bureau of statistics to-morrow morning and find out how many radios had been sold in the month of February of this year.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: You must still prove possession.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I quite agree that you must prove possession. You know a radio has been sold to a certain man, and you know his address. I still say that though there may be instances in which you would not be able to prove that a man had possession, as the lesser of two evils I believe the government would be well advised to abandon this granting of the power to search a man's house in connection with a radio.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I should like to give my point of view, as I understand this legislation. Of course, to follow the argument of the hon. member who just spoke we must compare this with other legislation passed during other regimes. Just recall legislation passed in connection with customs and excise, for example. Much drastic legislation has been passed in that regard.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: As far as I am concerned I am opposed to drastic legislation. We love liberty, and if there are people in this country who love liberty more than others it is those represented on this side of the house.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Liberty to break the law.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: No, not liberty in that sense; liberty to do good.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Who is to judge?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
