subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
And if you have no
conscience?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: As far as I am concerned I am ready to admit that I may have the least sensitive conscience on this side of the house, but still it might compare favourably with those of others. Let us come back to the point. This legislation seems a little drastic; I am ready to admit that, because of my love of liberty for the citizen.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: What about the padlock law?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
We shall talk about the
padlock law later on. The trend of thought and the policies of both parties since confederation have been based on experience. How could the Department of Transport deal with this matter of radio licences except by having regard to the experience of other departments, such as the Department of National Revenue, for instance. The hon. member who just spoke is an eminent lawyer from Toronto; I shall not call him ignorant, as he called me. I admire him for his ability, and he knows perfectly well that under the customs and excise legislation, for example, a person who has in his car smuggled goods or goods which are prohibited by law may have his car seized and confiscated as a result of having such goods in his possession. That is drastic law. That is a law which is repugnant to the spirit of liberty. Those are laws which have been passed by the party to which the hon. member belongs just as much as by the party now in power, and arise out of experience.
In the present instance I ask, as the Minister of Transport has done, how we can find out that a citizen has a radio set in his house, if we do not go into that house. How can the country collect the licence fee due it if the officer charged with the collection of fees cannot enter a house where he believes a fee is due? I am sure the hon. member who has just spoken is honest and wishes the citizens of Canada to pay their licence fees, but after listening to him our conclusion must be that he is trying to encourage the citizens of Canada to evade or to break the law. Otherwise the hon. member would agree with the minister, particularly in view of legislation adopted under other circumstances by this chamber. After all, I believe there is no citizen who is unwilling to pay a licence fee for his radio set in his house. If there are any such people, I believe we shall find them in the ranks of those who are encouraged by the observations of the hon. member, and who have a desire to evade the law. It may be that they would not be willing to permit the officer from the department to search their houses.
While I am on my feet may I say that I should have liked to see the licence fees for automobile radios reduced, because, so far as Quebec is concerned-and I believe all the provinces are in a somewhat similar situation-the people use their automobiles at most for only six months in the year. Consequently we would not avail ourselves of the use of our automobile radios to as great an extent, and I suggest it would be only fair to reduce the fee to one dollar a year. I made that submission before the committee which considered radio problems, and I believe it is my
Radio Broadcasting

duty to repeat it in this committee. I am sure the Minister of Transport has discussed this very important matter with the cabinet, the members of which represent Canada from east to west. I have enough faith in my superiors to abide by their decisions because, after all, it is not more pleasant for a member of the cabinet than for a private member to adopt unpopular legislation. My personal opinion is that a reduction to one dollar in the case of automobile licence fees would have been preferable, and I believe that view is shared by many other people. However, the position is that the cabinet has decided it is not possible to do that and, having a fair understanding of the difficulties experienced by the members of this or any other cabinet, I am content to abide by their decision.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
The consideration of
section 9 involves a review of the other sections of the measure, because in order to understand and appreciate this section we must read it in the light of other provisions. With that in mind I would refer the committee to paragraph (e) of section 4:
(e) prescribing that no radio receiving set or radio apparatus for installation or use as, or in, a private receiving station may be sold or serviced by any person until a licence is first obtained for such station.
When we refer to the opposite page in the bill we find that this is a new paragraph. I do not know whether the minister is considering an amendment or change in the section, or whether it stands for consideration.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: For the moment it stands.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I thought so. I would point out that in that paragraph we have a new provision which would appear to be a very complete check on radio sets. The official of the department charged with the collection of licence fees has in his hands or at his command a source of information in addition to that which he had under the former act. If the section is to remain whereby one who goes to a house to make a temporary repair, no matter how trivial it may be upon a radio, must see that a licence has been taken out for that radio, then I do not see how anyone can escape without rendering it necessary to make use of the drastic remedy of a search warrant. The minister may point out that this provision appeared in substantially the same form in the previous act. I see that it has been redrawn, reworded and recast in some respects. My point is, however, that the minister has provided additional drastic and effective checks upon the issue of radio licences, and that the agent charged with the collection of licence fees now has at

his disposal information he did not have before and information which, I submit, will enable him in a very large measure without a search warrant to find out whether or not licences have been taken out. I do not know what the minister proposes to do with respect to the section which stands, but I think it is fair at this stage to point out to the committee the situation which will exist if the section passes.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite are endeavouring to point out that this is all new legislation, and that it has never been in effect before. In reply to that may I say that I have in my hand a regulation signed by Alfred Duranleau, Minister of Marine, and dated at Ottawa on June 16, 1932. While I refer to this regulation I would ask the hon. member to cast his eye along paragraph (e) of section 4 to which he has referred. The regulation I have before me is in these words:
6. (c) No person shall sell any radio receiving set to any person for installation or operation until the purchaser has produced for inspection of the vendor his private radio receiving licence.
(d) No person shall service a radio receiving set until the owner thereof produces to such person his licence to operate such set.
My hon. friends opposite had exactly the same legislation. We have not changed their legislation one iota. In 1932 hon. gentlemen opposite enforced the collection of radio licence fees by search warrants and the sending of police officers into people's homes. This practice has continued since then. The practice of the department has been built up. on what hon. gentlemen opposite started in 1932. We have not been able to find a substitute method which could be put into force without causing a considerable drop in revenue and tremendous injustice to those who pay willingly. There is a certain section of the population who will not pay unless there is some form of compulsion. I wish we could find some other system. Every year I bring the officers of the department charged with collecting these licence fees into conference to see if at the end of the year they have not found some variation to the existing system which will produce the same or better results. But we have not been able to find such a variation. We are not passing new legislation; we are continuing the legislation that was in force in 1932, 1933, 1934 and 1935 when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. The practice was started by hon. gentlemen opposite; it was built up by them, and we have been unable to find a substitute.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I cannot see anything particularly wrong with this section. The

Radio Broadcasting
2S21
hon. member for Yorfc South (Mr. Lawson) has told us that ninety-nine per cent of the radio owners would give voluntary information when an official came to their homes.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I am sorry, but I did not make that statement.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: What percentage did the hon. member mention? I thought he said ninety-nine per cent.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: The hon. member is right as far as the percentage is concerned, but the rest of the statement is wrong.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: I believe that ninety-nine per cent of the people would answer truthfully when an officer came to them and asked if they had a radio. This section was intended to deal with the one per cent of the population who would not answer truthfully. It would be only in a few instances that this section would be enforced. I agree with the hon. member that ninety-nine per oent of the people would disclose that they had radios and, if they had no licence, would be ready to give excuses. It may be contended that we would not be losing much revenue by not enforcing this section, but that is not the question. If a radio owner can escape paying his licence fee, the news soon spreads and his neighbours will say, "If he does not pay, then we will not." The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) has said that paragraph (e) of section 4 would provide a complete check, but it seems to me that there are instances where that paragraph would not work. Suppose I buy a radio; the dealer who sells it to me would hand in my name and address. But suppose I use it for a month or so and give it to my neighbour, my brother or my mother; I am not a seller and I do not have to report to the departs ment. Where would the check be?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: Would not your sister or your mother be a person?

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: But I would not be a seller.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: It says, "By any person."

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext: "May he sold." When I buy it they have a check on me, but in the instance I mentioned I would not be the seller. I am giving away the radio.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
Section 9 provides that a justice of the peace may issue a search warrant when there is reasonable ground for believing that a private receiving station has been established without a licence. I contend that this section places too great a power
in the hands of a justice of the peace. In many municipalities the aldermen have the right to be appointed justices of the peace and from time to time these appointments are cancelled. Many people in this country look upon their home as a castle and they are going to resent these search warrants being issued. Some of them are likely to take exception to the search being made and we may have violence and other forms of trouble. We are granting the right to issue a search warrant for the collection of $2 or $2.50.
If it is thought necessary to have search warrants issued, then I submit the power to issue should be placed only in the hands of officials appointed by the federal Department of Justice. We should not have the promiscuous searching of homes when only $2.50 is to be collected. To my mind this provision is too wide. I have heard the discussion on both sides of the house in connection with this section, and according to hon. members opposite the principal reason for its being in this bill is the fact that in 1932, 1933, 1934 and 1935 the members of one political party enacted similar legislation and therefore it must be all right. This legislation is before us for revision and these various matters should be looked into. The question of whether this section is right or wrong should not be governed by the fact that similar legislation was enacted previously. I ask the minister to look at this matter fairly and not make it so easy to obtain a search warrant.

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
I should like to make two suggestions to the minister. The first is whether it would not be better to change the phrase "justice of the peace" to "a police magistrate" or some person having some legal training, I am not familiar with the other provinces; but I know that in the province from which I come men are appointed as justices of the peace who have no legal training, who, in some instances, have little if any training of any sort, because in a small community some man must be found who can take oaths and that sort of thing, and a man is given the appointment. I know many such who-I say this with all deference are not in a position to pass judgment in a case like this as to whether a search warrant should or should not be issued. I appreciate the minister's difficulty; I recognize that you must prove possession, and to prove possession you must enter a person's home, but I believe it would lead to a lot of troublesome meddling if you gave that right to some men who have not any training and are perhaps not in a position to exercise fair judgment.

Radio Broadcasting

I also refer the minister to the clause, "he may grant a search warrant to any police officer or any officer appointed in that behalf by the minister." I can understand the latter phrase, "any officer appointed in that behalf by the minister," but as to "any police officer," I am not just clear why that should be permitted. I think it should read, "any police officer authorized by the minister or asked by those authorized to make collection of this licence fee"; any police officer at their request might act. But to allow any police officer authorized by any justice of the peace to do so might lead, it seems to me, to meddlesome trouble-making in small, minor districts where personalities and little local quarrels might intrude, and give the minister a great deal more trouble than he has, and I know he is anxious to avoid that. I therefore suggest that the phrase "justice of the peace" might be changed, unless there is some good reason why it should not, and that the other phrase should read, "any police officer appointed in that behalf by the minister," leaving out the first part of it, "any police officer".

subtopic: REVISION OP RADIOTELEGRAPH ACT-CLARIFYING OF SECTIONS DEALING WITH LICENSING RADIO RECEIVING SETS
speechtext:
The minister stated a few moments ago that this system was started by the late government in 1932. It does not matter to me for one moment whether it was started in 1932 or not. I might suggest that two wrongs do not make a right, and if the late government made a mistake in instituting the present system that is no reason why this government should carry it on. Personally I am absolutely opposed to the fee of $2.50 for a radio. I believe it would be well, if a yearly fee is to be charged, to charge $1 a year for the first radio and $2 or $2.50 for any additional radio in any one household. That would make it easier for the small householder.
I have another suggestion to offer, that it might be well to charge the tax on radios at their source; that is, charge the manufacturer or the selling source. It would cease to be a nuisance tax; the person buying a radio would be prepared to pay a certain price for it, and when that price was paid that would be the last expenditure he would have to make for it. I am opposed to this annual tax. It is a nuisance tax. The government well know it and they are sorry they are mixed up in it.

speechtext:

Why should there be so large

The increase in travelling expenses is largely accounted for by the fact that the staff is larger and that there are

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
more people moving about in connection with those inquiries. Much of the increased economic work is due to the expansion of marketing activities.
The minister provides for a chief of markets information service. I assume this is a new appointment. Does this not come into conflict with the Department of Trade and Commerce?
No, it does not.

Will the minister be
good enough to give us an outline of the nature of the work performed by the economics branch of the department? There are two problems in which I am particularly interested. Speaking from the standpoint of Ontario, I believe that conditions are changing, and the old 100-acre farm seems destined to pass away. Has the economics branch considered what is the optimum size for an Ontario farm; that is, what size of farm is the most efficient unit of operation? Is it 100, 300 or 500 acres? Has any study been made along that line, and is any information available?
The agricultural implement companies are steadily tending towards the production of larger sized implements, looking in the direction of power farming, and this is leading to the larger sized unit of farm. If the department could work out an analysis of this question which would help to determine the size of farm that would be most profitable, I think it would be a sound contribution to Canadian agriculture.
There is one more problem to which the department might possibly give some attention. It is extremely difficult to secure any details in regard to the earnings of Canadian farmers. We have a record of the earnings of civil servants; we have a record of the wages of the men who work in industry; but because the farm situation is much more complex, and the farmer gets his living on the farm, it is extremely difficult to secure adequate information. It could be done only by a close and detailed analysis over a sufficient number of farms so that we might have some actual insight into the real situation. This would be valuable to agriculture in more ways than one, because it would give some idea of what the farmer actually earns, and it would be valuable information to some of the people engaged in other industries. Moreover, from the standpoint of the farmer himself, it would give him certain necessary information which would be helpful to him. Jim Hill once said that if you are in business and cannot find out what profit you are
making, it would be better for you to go out of that business. If some of the farmers knew the real situation as it is to-day, they would be more keen in the pursuit of their own interests and find means of improving the conditions on their farms, and if other classes knew what the farmer was earning, then perhaps there might be a broader measure of sympathy in considering the problems of agriculture.

The activities of the
economics branch are to some extent along the line advocated by the hon. member. Most of the work undertaken is done on the invitation of, and in cooperation with the provincial departments. The reason for this is obvious. Much of the inquiry has to be made on lands that are privately owned, most of which are under the control of the provinces, and even where it is crown lands that are being examined they are under provincial control.
A few years ago there was in Ontario an investigation of the sort suggested by the hon. gentleman. It was carried out under the direction of the college of agriculture at Guelph, and as a result there is some information which has been regarded as standard up to the present time. It is possible that there is need for another inquiry into the size of farm that can be operated most successfully by the average farmer in Ontario, but any request for such an investigation would naturally come from the province. We set up the machinery for making inquiries of this kind largely because of the impossibility of nine different organizations in Canada conducting such work, and also because of the expense. There would be no way of getting proper comparisons between the activities carried on in one section and those carried on in another if the work were done under a number of different authorities. The department here has therefore attempted to build up an organization which can cooperate with the different provinces.
Some of the work being carried on at the present time is done in western Canada in connection with the land utilization plans, and inquiries are being conducted in cooperation with the governments of the different provinces. Economics research work covers a fairly wide field including research and general marketing problems; the study of costs of distributing fruits and vegetables; making an annual analysis of the farmers' cooperative marketing enterprises; cooperative purchase of farm supplies. Another phase of research in marketing is that of analysing marketing problems in Toronto and Ottawa, and studies

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
are being conducted into the consumption of milk, cheese, cream and meats. The purpose is to appraise the facts affecting consumption of farm products. This division also directs research in land utilization in the west. These studies are confined to the drought area and are concerned with the economic utilization of land in Saskatchewan and Alberta. In addition to this, the division makes studies with regard to the cost of milk production in Ontario and factors affecting the price of Nova Scotia apples. They also get out a number of publications dealing with different subjects that have been investigated.
What relationship has the chief of transportation to the economics branch?

Transportation is naturally a very important part of marketing. The product is drawn usually from a considerable distance; that is, the surplus that has to be sold and shipped is produced at a considerable distance from the place where it is consumed. There are very many problems affecting the farmers from one end of the country to the other, problems having to do with cost of shipment, particularly local freight costs, where, because of some new development, the freight is travelling in different directions from the route it usually follows. When these conditions arise we have someone available to make inquiries and, on behalf of the farming communities, to present the case properly to the different transportation organizations.

Is there any discrimination in the rates on fruits going from British Columbia into the prairie provinces as compared with the rates on fruit going from Nova Scotia, particularly in carload lots? I understand that in order to get the cheaper rate from British Columbia, the quantity must be something like 60,000 pounds, while for a similar rate from Nova Scotia, it is only about 30,000 pounds. Has there been any investigation in that respect?

I am not sure of the facts with regard to the regular rates as between the maritime provinces and the prairie country as compared with the rates from British Columbia to the prairies. Last fall we got a special rate on apples shipped from Nova Scotia to the prairies. By getting the special rate from Nova Scotia we were able to lay apples down in the prairies at a slightly lower cost than the apples from British Columbia cost.

I listened with interest to
what the hon. member for Huron North

(Mr. Deachman) said concerning the condition of agriculture and the state of the farmers generally, and particularly in eastern Canada. It has been truly said that if the farmer were to keep books and charge up the same labour and other costs that manufacturing industries do, he would never put a plough in the ground, because, he could never show a profit. But although he cannot show profits from a bookkeeping standpoint, he seems to get along, although I fully agree with what the hon. member said about his position at the present time.
How far does the federal administration deal with domestic marketing? I understand that, under the constitution, trade within the country is purely a provincial matter; yet it seeims that our federal department does make investigations into domestic' marketing. I should also like to know what attention is being paid by the department to cooperative efforts in agriculture. It seems to me a very important branch of marketing, and every effort by farmers towards cooperative marketing of their products should be fostered and assisted as far as possible by the federal department. What assistance is being given to farmers' cooperative organizations throughout the dominion?

There is some difficulty in regulating the marketing of farm products from a federal centre. This was realized when the Natural Products Marketing Act was referred to the supreme court. However, it is recognized by the provincial governments that a large part of the work, particularly that having to do with the regulations covering standardization of products, can be done better by a central organization than by nine different authorities. The result is that even where the constitution does not permit of our taking action to enforce certain regulations, the provinces cooperate with us by naming our officials to be their officials in many instances to do that work. While we pay these men who conduct the work, they are acting in some circumstances as appointees of the provinces as well. There has been no difficulty in preventing overlapping in connection with work of that kind. It is fully realized by the provincial authorities that if a product is produced in one province and sold in another there must be a good deal of cooperation.
As far as farmers' cooperatives are concerned there is no other work I can speak of at the moment than that of issuing information through this economics branch as to what has been done elsewhere in connection with the development of farmers'

I wish to make a plea for the potato growers of Prince Edward Island. For the last few years they have been largely dependent upon the growing of potatoes for which they have to find a market outside. Under a previous vote we found that there is quite a staff in Great Britain looking after the marketing of our produce. Last year I was over there, and it is a fact that We have to fight our way into that market, because the British farmer is looking out for himself and does not wish to allow any more of our products to come in than can be avoided. But they want to buy certain products, which we have in abundance. I refer to all kinds of grain. The British farmer does not want to use his land for growing grain because he can get better returns from live stock. He is willing to let us grow the grain here and ship it to him. But our potatoes have always been shut out of the British market; there has been a total embargo. I do not understand why we could not overcome that in some way. The reason the British Department of Agriculture gave is that we have the potato beetle in Canada, and it might be carried over there and the country become infested with it. I have pleaded before this that the department have a real investigation made into this question. I do not believe that the potato beetle could be introduced into Great Britain in that way. They receive potatoes shipped from different European countries where the beetle has been for years, and where, in fact, it is said to have originated. If the potato beetle could thrive in Great Britain, it would have been established there long ago, because these insects are great travellers.
In all fairness, in view of the amount of goods we purchase from Great Britain, the Department of Agriculture should again take up the question of the lifting of this embargo. A few years ago we made a determined effort to prove that it would be impossible for the potato beetle to be carried over there in potato sacks. In New Brunswick they even went so far as to put in brushing machines, the potatoes are carefully graded and brushed, every potato inspected, and the bags carefully inspected and sealed. Notwithstanding that, we were unable to get our potatoes admitted to the market. There must be some other reason than the potato beetle. I made extensive inquiries while I was over there, and the tremendous amount of potatoes imported into Great Britain was a surprise to me. In
all fairness, Canadians are entitled to a share of that business. I believe if the matter were taken up by the minister, he might be able to obtain something in the way of a satisfactory agreement with them so that our potatoes might get into that market. We are endeavouring to process potatoes, putting them up in cans, and I understand that venture is meeting with a great deal of success, but still the same problem confronts the farmer. This year he had practically to give away his potatoes, to sell them below cost of production.
You grew too many; that was all.

We grow potatoes because in the past they have been a good cash crop. I agree that perhaps we should get back more to the mixed farming that was carried on years ago, and the department of agriculture of Prince Edward Island has been urging the farmers to do so. But there were good years when the farmers made a good deal of money out. of potatoes; they have started off on this line of farming, and they seem anxious to stick to it. There is another market that we are always hoping to regain; that is the Cuban market. I know it is not the function of the Minister of Agriculture to negotiate treaties with foreign countries, but it is a very important part of the work of the Department of Agriculture to endeavour to find markets for the products of the farmers of this country. I wish the minister would take up with his colleagues the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of National Revenue the possibility of something being done to bring about a trade agreement with Cuba and some of those other countries in South America and the West Indies. I should like to hear from the minister what hopes he has of getting into the British market.

About a year and a half ago, the government of the province of New Brunswick sent a man to the South American countries in order to explore market possibilities there. At that time we did not have either the facilities or the funds to assist in that work, but last year we appointed a representative to go to the South American countries and explore the possibilities of creating a market for potatoes throughout all the countries in which it is possible for our seed potatoes to be sold. As a result of the activities of the provincial man or men, of our trade commissioners in the different countries and of the representative of our own department, who was able to discuss with these

people not so much the marketing but the different varieties that we produce, the proper way to plant and care for them and how to fight the diseases that are associated with our potato crop, the sale of our seed potatoes in South America has been greatly promoted. Speaking from memory, I think somewhere in the neighbourhood of seven hundred thousand cases of potatoes were sold in South America following those activities. This year we have sent the same man to Europe, and more particularly to Great Britain, to carry on activities similar to those he carried on last year in South America and the West Indies.
Who was that man?

Mr. Arkell, who was
previously in the department. I may say that I have had quite a number of communications from different countries in South America commenting very favourably upon the experience they had with our official while he was there, not from the point of view of promoting trade but because he was able to discuss with them general agricultural problems, and to give them the benefit of the experiences of the department here in different lines of agriculture, more particularly in connection with the growing of potatoes. As I said, within the last two weeks he left for Great Britain, and our agricultural commissioner left this week for the same country. These two gentlemen will immediately take up such problems as those just referred to by the hon. member for Prince, and I am sure that some beneficial results will come from the activities now being carried on.

I was greatly interested in
the statement just made by the minister, to the effect that other gentlemen, in addition to those who were over there last summer to investigate marketing conditions in Great Britain and other parts of the empire, have been sent-on a fairly good salary, I believe -to investigate certain matters. I just asked the minister the name of one of these gentlemen, and I find that I know him of old. He is an estimable gentleman who at one time occupied a very high position in the Department of Agriculture. But I wonder if it was necessary to undertake this extra expense at this time in connection with these activities. Not only have we had a commission investigating marketing in Great Britain; we have our trade commissioners there and in other parts of the world, whose duty it is to undertake just the sort of work that Mr. Arkell has been called upon to do. It seems to me that the work is more or less overlapping, and it would appear hardly TMr. Gardiner.]
necessary to make such extra expenditure for this purpose. However, I suppose it is impossible at the moment to have anything done about the matter.
Before I sit down I should like to ask the minister one other question. I understand that the set-up of the marketing division has already been discussed to a certain extent; but in the estimates I notice provision for an assistant director of marketing services, at a fairly good salary, under this branch of agricultural economics. In addition, I was going to ask the minister, when the administration vote was up, about the provision for a special poultry commissioner, also at a very fair salary. In the old days we had gentlemen at the heads of the different branches of agriculture. We had a dairy commissioner, a live stock commissioner, a head of the sheep and swine division, and so on. I do not see those names mentioned in the present set-up. I am wondering if these gentlemen have been demoted or, if not, just what their position is to-day. They were perhaps the best available men within the department at the time, and it may be that their positions are differently described to-day; but in any event I think the minister might at this time give us some idea of the standing of these gentlemen, whether they are still heads of the different departments, or whether they have been absorbed in the general rearrangement and have no official standing at the present time.

In reply to the first part of my hon. friend's remarks, the part of the work which cannot be done properly by officials located at particular points, whether agricultural or trade commissioners, is the matter of checking on efforts that are being put forth by those selling similar commodities in other parts of the world. For example, Mr. Arkell has just been in South America, where he found that most of the seed potatoes which do not come from Canada or the United States come from Holland, Germany or some other European country. We have found that there are certain advantages-at least he and the others who have gone to South America have so found-in the Canadian seed. It has been found also that some excellent varieties are produced in some of the other countries and shipped to South America for seed. Part of the work we intend to do in Europe is to have these men, particularly those working under Mr. Allen, who has been sent over there recently and who is an expert in many of these lines, examine into the activities carried on in these countries and, if any varieties or methods can be found that might

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
be used to advantage in Canada, to have them tried out on our. experimental farms here and, if possible, to develop those lines in Canada. Mr. Arkell, having examined into the activities in the South American countries will, in turn, examine into the activities in the countries in which those varieties of seed originated, and will be in a much better position to give advice to the department as to what we ought to do by way of experimentation than would any individual who may be established permanently in any one place. It is work of that kind which is being done by Mr. Arkell, and any others who may be sent. It is not a matter of inquiring into marketing possibilities, in the sense that we sent a committee last year to England for the purpose of making inquiries; rather it is an inquiry into the agricultural possibilities, generally, a matter of working in cooperation with our commissioners and bringing back information which can be made available to organizations in this country.
As I said at the beginning of the discussion on the estimates we have set up four different divisions. There is the marketing division, the production division, the experimental division and the research division, and there is a director for each of them. In so far as any of the original branches of the department can be associated with one or another of these divisions, this is done. A section of a branch which is not properly allied with the work being done in connection with marketing, for example, but more closely allied with production, is placed in the production division. But, so far as economics is concerned, may I say in reply to an inquiry which was made that the assistant director is Doctor Booth, who was previously in charge of the economics branch of the department. His classification in the department, so far as salary and general position are concerned, is exactly the same now as it was before.

What
classification has Mr. Arkell?
He is just engaged temporarily from time to time, at a certain wage, and is given expenses in addition to his salary.

I do not wish to take up too much time, nor do I wish to criticize the setup of the department or the work that is being done. In fact, I believe most of the work is being carried on in an excellent manner and,, further, I believe that a good deal of the work is necessary. But I still cannot understand why it is necessary to send
special representatives to these foreign countries and to the British market when we already have estimable gentlemen there representing the Department of Trade and Commerce whose specific duty it is to look into the very matters that Mr. Arkell and the other special representatives who are sent over there look into. It seems to me there must be a certain amount of overlapping, and if there is any overlapping it may be that any misunderstanding which may have existed between the departments will continue to exist. When the minister was speaking about Mr. Arkell he used the expression, "or any others who may be sent." Does the minister anticipate that any other men, whether they have special qualifications or not, are likely to be sent within the near future to assist the organization already in existence in Great Britain and other countries? Will they be undertaking special missions of the kind Mr. Arkell pursued, in days gone by and is pursuing at the present time? If anything of that sort is anticipated, I think the minister should frankly tell the committee about it.

We do not have anything in mind at this time in addition to what is now being carried on in that direction. But, as a result of information we get back from people there, it may be necessary to send experts in certain lines.
At page 104 of the report it is indicated that there was a study of the cost of milk production in Ontario in 1937. What are the results of that study?

The investigation in
connection with milk in Ontario is still continuing, and the results are not yet available for publication.

I have listened to the
minister's observations respecting the reorganization of his department. To what extent have the activities of that department been expanded? Am I correct in assuming the work that is now being done was, in some measure at least, performed in the past, but through different agencies, and that he has just rearranged and realigned duties which were formerly assigned to other employees or officials? To what extent is he embarking on any new or untried policy which was not, at least to some extent, being carried on before he undertook to reorganize? We have heard u great deal about reorganization, reclassification and rearrangement. As I understand the situation, practically all of the work now being done was done before. Possibly it was done by other officials, but what I do want to have is a concise and clear explanation of

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
the expansion of or any new development in the work of his department which has followed or will follow as a result of the reorganization.
It is reconsideration, not reorganization.

I think it will be
remembered by hon. members that on the first evening we discussed the estimates of the Department of Agriculture I explained that the reorganization was for the convenience of the administration in operating the department. The Department of Agriculture, like other departments of government in Canada, has grown up since confederation-
And is still getting bigger.

Yes, bigger and better. I believe other ministers in the department have had in mind the thought that there should be some reorganization. When I took over the department I was satisfied that was so, and the reorganization was done in as direct a manner as was possible. We took longer in bringing it about than I had hoped would be necessary, but I believe that was to be expected in dealing with an organization as widespread as the dominion Department of Agriculture. The main expansion has been in connection with marketing activities. Other branches have been made to relate themselves to our greater efforts in connection with marketing. As I said the other evening, in the first place we did research work to discover other organizations, whether in Canada or out of it, with which we might associate ourselves in order to bring to bear upon agriculture in this country all the scientific and other discoveries it was possible to find in connection with agriculture.
Is that new?

No; that is not a new undertaking, but we did that in the first instance. We earned our activities to the experimental farms, as has always been done. We are still carrying on our activities in connection with production, as has always been done, but we are going one step farther and are emphasizing the necessity for greater care in connection with marketing.
I agree with the statement made the other evening by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) that the most important efforts along that lane will have to be made in Canada itself. The greater part of our farm products is sold and marketed in this country. Only cheese, wheat and possibly apples and bacon are sold in considerable volume, as

compared with entire production, outside Canada. For that reason our activities will be continued in Canada in connection with promoting the sale of these products and increasing consumption by producing better standards. I may say that I know of no activity, either within or without Canada, that has to do with the selling of products. We have no sales organization. In so far as agriculture is concerned, our activities outside Canada have been expended in another direction. We have sent overseas a man who is recognized throughout Canada as an agricultural expert. He has the ability to go into any agricultural educational institution on the other side, acquaint himself with their activities and make known to our agricultural colleges and other institutions the possibilities of growing certain products now being produced on the European continent and in Great Britain. This gentleman speaks two or three of the languages of the people in those countries. I believe having a man in touch with activities on the other side is a new idea.

I believe the minister appreciates and sympathizes with the objectives of the Natural Products Marketing Act. That act had as an objective the improvement of the quality of our products at home and the providing of better marketing facilities abroad. Have the objectives of that act been kept in mind and has a way been found to carry them into effect? That legislation had a rather unfortunate fate before the courts, but I believe the minister will agree that its Objectives were sound and in the interests of agriculture. Perhaps the minister has studied other methods by which the same objectives could be reached. Has that been the policy of the department or have the objectives of that act been scrapped altogether? Are we proceeding along new lines to attain the desirable results which were in view when that legislation was enacted?

Earlier in the afternoon we listened to a discussion on dairying matters as they were related to the Natural Products Marketing Act. For example, the province of Ontario carried on certain activities in the latter part of 1935 and in 1936 in connection with the cheese producers' organization. These activities were carried on under the Natural Products Marketing Act. This organization was empowered to charge five cents per 100 pounds.

That was provincial,
absolutely.

Originally it was federal. When the Natural Products Marketing Act

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
was declared ultra vires, the cheese producers' organization made application to this government for a grant of $8,000 in order to continue the activities started under the act but for which collections could not be made. We had to accept some responsibility as a federal government for what had been set up under the Natural Products Marketing Act, and we made a grant of $5,000, which was used by the organization to assist in paying an official whom they had sent over to Great Britain. We did not give a grant in 1937 as we did not assume any responsibility for that year. After our act was declared ultra vires, the provincial government passed an act empowering producers' organizations in Ontario to collect fees similar to those which had been collected under the Natural Products Marketing Act. I am not sure whether we have had applications for assistance since then, but I know none has been given. The report which was read to the committee this afternoon indicated that the $5,000 was paid in 1937, but it was paid in our financial year 1936-37. It just happened to go into their treasury after December 31, 1936.
I think this illustrates what has been done as a result of the finding in connection with the Natural Products Marketing Act. The province of Ontario has taken action in connection with cheese and, I believe, some other commodities. New Brunswick and British Columbia have both taken action in connection with certain products. These three provinces have taken action which makes it possible for certain products to be marketed under schemes similar to those set up under the Natural Products Marketing Act. So far as the federal department is concerned, we realize that we have certain obligations, particularly in connection with the marketing of products in other countries and interpro-vincially.
And in grading.

We have a perfect right to do that under the constitution. We have endeavoured to create the best possible sentiment among our customers by seeing to it that they get a superior commodity; that is, we are trying to standardize and raise the quality of our products. We are trying to place in the hands of the consumer a product with which he will be satisfied, no matter what may be the marketing facilities which place that product at his disposal. I believe we are getting fairly good results from these activities.

I was interested in the
remarks of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) in connection with the efforts being
made to sell potatoes in South America and Cuba. The hon. member asked the minister what possibilities there were of selling potatoes in Cuba, but I do not believe the minister gave an answer. The potato growers of the maritime provinces are very much interested in the possibilities of selling potatoes in Cuba. During the last few years a certain portion of the press in the maritime provinces has been stating that a great market for our potatoes exists in Cuba. Then we hear that the farmers in Cuba can raise enough potatoes to supply that market. We hear also that the reason why we are not selling potatoes to Cuba is that a dumping duty has been placed against Cuban sugar. I think it would be a splendid thing if the minister would tell the committee, and through the committee the people of these provinces, whether there is a market in Cuba for New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island potatoes. I should also like to know if Mr. Arkell, who was investigating conditions in South America, Cuba and the West Indies, has made a report as to the prospect of future sales of seed and table potatoes in those countries. It is all very well for the agent to go down and investigate; but unless the people are informed as to the result of this investigation and unless he finds some market for their product, I would not consider that his activities had been of very much use. I know we have been selling a great many seed potatoes in South America recently; but in the maritime provinces there are not so many producers of seed potatoes as there are producers of the table potato, and what agitates the minds of most of the farmers in connection with the sale of the potato is not only the seed, potato but also the table potato, of which, as everyone knows, we in the maritime provinces can raise the best in Canada, possibly in the world. If the minister would kindly answer these questions, I think it would satisfy many of the farmers in my own province of New Brunswick and in the neighbouring province of Prince Edward Island.
I should also like to know whether the department at Ottawa is cooperating with the departments in the various provinces. New Brunswick, for instance, sends agents down south nearly every year, and we hear of the federal department sending their agents there also. It seems to me that if there were cooperation it would not be necessary for so many of these men to be travelling all over the world at the expense of the federal and provincial governments. Fewer men and better

Supply-Agriculture-Economics
results would be better for the governments, for the country and for the farmers who are more interested in selling their products than in reports.

Mr. Arkell, who was down there last year and made inquiries with regard to the possibilities of markets for both table potaoes and seed potatoes in the South American and West Indian countries, reported back to the government here first what he found in those countries. Then he went from here to the different capitals of the provinces where potatoes are grown in great volume, but particularly to the capitals of the maritime provinces, made separate reports to their governments, and met the representatives of different organizations that are interested in the marketing of potatoes in those countries.
Was this report published?

His report has not been published, but any of his findings are available to the authorities in the provinces. In addition to that, he made reports to us somewhat along the lines of the discussion which has now started, that is reports as to whether it would be advisable in years to come to promote the sale of seed potatoes in certain countries as against promoting the sale of table potatoes. There are certain parts of South America where, we understand from the reports made to us, seed' potatoes can be grown to advantage. When those countries develop the growing of seed potatoes we, of course, being further away from those countries, shall probably find -that we shall lose a market rather than gain one by promoting, for the time being, the sale of seed potatoes there. We are benefiting as much as we can by information of that kind in directing others who may be intending to develop markets in any particular countries in South America.
In addition to that, the men who have been sent down by the different provinces, particularly by New Brunswick, have been sent to promote the sale of the potatoes of their particular province in South American countries. When our potatoes have gone down there, there have developed, in connection with certain varieties, certain diseases. The provincial authority has then made application to* the federal authority, as the latter is the only authority which has experts who can go down to deal with a problem of that kind, and we have now a man in South America dealing with a disease which developed there in connection with potatoes shipped from

the maritimes, a disease which, I understand, did not prevail in this country before the potatoes went to South America, but has developed within the potatoes there with new conditions existing. We have found, from the first report received from our representative, that he has proven to the satisfaction of the South American people that this disease did not have its origin in Canada, because the same disease is prevalent among potatoes the seed of which was obtained from European countries.
It is that kind of work which is being done. If we did not have representatives down there to deal with the matter on the spot, at the moment the disease develops, it would be very simple for other countries to convince people there that this disease was introduced through the introduction of a new variety of potatoes from Canada, and if that were the case we should immediately find ourselves in exactly the same position in those countries as we are in Great Britain, by reason of their objection to our potatoes because we have potato bugs in this country. We do not want a situation of that kind to develop, so we think it is good business from the agricultural point of view to send men down, when the provinces ask that they be sent, in order to check up on any diseases which develop in connection with any province.

Well, now, will the minister kindly answer the question with reference to the possibility of markets in the island of Cuba? In the maritime provinces, because we used to sell great quantities of potatoes to Cuba, there prevails an impression that that market, were it not for certain duties, would be open for our potatoes and could take very large quantities.
Mi'. GARDINER:	I think I said some
little time ago that there was really no overlapping between our department and the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I do not want to get into a discussion with regard to trade agreements. In so far as trade agreements and tariffs on different items affecting agricultural products are concerned, I do not intend, under these estimates, to get into a discussion of that question. I can only say that, as I understand it, there is a question in the minds of potato growers in the maritime provinces as to which line of development would be most beneficial to them, whether to promote largely the sale of seed or to promote mainly the sale of table potatoes. With that discussion the people of the maritimes are much more familiar than

I am. There is a question in the minds of all those who go down there as to whether the people in Cuba can maintain the production of potatoes at the present level as a result of having imported into that country seed potatoes from Canada and other northern countries. I am not at the moment in a position to answer the question as to which would pay the maritime people best. At the present time there is a market for both kinds of potatoes.

I commend the Minister of Agriculture for the addition to the program this year, because it seems to me that this is the psychological time to develop Our marketing facilities, especially in Great Britain and the countries of northwestern Europe. As the committee knows, those countries are suffering to-day from drought and will need this year a great many more of our products than formerly; and no doubt next year, when we look over the departmental reports, we shall find that the Department of Agriculture will have a glowing statement showing the tremendous increases of exports, especially to Britain and Germany, if they develop those markets, because the demand exists, the people need the goods, and anybody can sell them to them. This is the psychological moment to press this sales agency idea, because we are getting away from that conception of the past when holding policies of various organizations in Canada more or less restricted the purchasing power of those other countries. Because of the antipathy towards us, these people tightened their belts and used black instead of white bread. To-day we have an entirely different picture facing us. It seems to me that these agencies have been organized at the right time, and now we want results.
The minister has mentioned four services; Marketing, production, experimentation and research work. As far as possible we should avoid overlapping between any of these services such as experimentation and research. The provinces are at present spending a tremendous sum on these services, but naturally the federal department could spend money profitably on marketing. We know this is likely to be our banner year, especially in western Canada, and we shall have potatoes, wheat, oats and other commodities in abundance. We want a market for these products, and this is the psychological moment for these efforts to be made. I suggest that a genuine effort be made to promote good will in obtaining these markets. The government should expand its services at this time. I also recommend to the minister a proper coordination of these various
services so that we may obtain from time to time the knowledge we require of what is going on. We trust that next year, through the increase in the grant, some good will result. The government has a glorious opportunity now, and I am sure that all hon. members, no matter to what party they belong, wish Canada prosperity. This is probably our year for obtaining it. As I say, the government has an excellent opportunity, and we hope that the best possible use will be made of the grant. We know that we can produce enough, but marketing is the end to which attention must be paid. That is the be all and end all of the industry.
I wonder if the committee would pass item 7? We have been discussing item 10 for the last hour.
With regard to the production of milk in Ontario, can the minister tell us when that investigation started, how long it will last, and who is carrying it on?

Investigations with
regard to milk in Ontario have been going on for two years. They are carried on under a cooperative arrangement involving the government of Ontario, the agricultural college at Guelph and the Department of Agriculture here, through the economics branch. It is being directed by our official here, and a similar official in Toronto, and will continue for a number of years. The investigation is one that requires records over a term of years if it is to be beneficial. I am not in a position to say how many years it will take to get sufficient records to be really valuable.
Is it being carried out on different farms throughout the country or merely at experimental stations?

On different farms
throughout the province in cooperation with the farmers and with their consent.
Just a stated number of farms in different localities?
There is a considerable number. It is not a matter of dividing it up among municipalities and saying that each municipality shall have so many. It is a matter of groups of farmers.
Different breeds?
The breed does not enter into the checking, but certain herds are checked.

Item No. 7 calls for $120,260 for the pursuit of agricultural economics. I take it that this is a necessary item, or this

and other governments would not vote money for it year after year. The number of employees has been increased from twelve to twenty and the amount of money by $47,000. I was not altogether satisfied with the minister's reply to an hon. member who spoke a few minutes ago as to the extent to which this will be a new service to the farmer and the extent to which it is an elaboration of an already existing service. Will the farmer on the back road feel the impact of any part of this $47,000?

This is 'based on activities begun in 1922. I believe the branch was set up about that time. Of course, it has been developing from then until the present day. The increase in staff this year is due to the demands that are being made on the branch from different parts of Canada, and the increase from $72,000 to $120,000 represents as nearly as possible the increase in activities along the lines we followed previously. Has there been any progress in connection with the new terminal market in Toronto?
As my hon. friend knows, an investigation was carried out and a report made to those interested in the market.

Have they asked for any assistance from the federal department in connection with the new terminal market in that city, and is there any intention on the part of the department to give that assistance?
We have no request for assistance of the kind indicated. We have requests for service, and we give whatever service we can, such as investigations and reports.

As the minister knows, we are faced with many economic problems in Saskatchewan, and I would say that some of the policies adopted by the present government will add to those problems. Under this item, what sort of work is being carried on in the western provinces? We have been discussing the marketing of our products and the question of advertising in other countries. Last fall at about the time that Professor Shaw was overseas on this work under the new branch-

Would my hon. friend
mind leaving that until we are on that item? It is item 12.

Under the item at present before the committee we have discussed nearly

everything in the line of marketing. The discussion has been along the lines of advertising our agricultural products.	At that
time the wheat board initiated a very extensive campaign in Great Britain advertising Canadian wheat. I understand Professor Shaw is a member of the wheat board as well. I am not suggesting that he is drawing two salaries, but the minister might explain his position. Did Professor Shaw, during his time over there last fall, take any part in this advertising scheme initiated under the wheat board?

Dean Shaw, as he was at the time of his appointment, was appointed to the wheat board in 1935, and has continued as a member of that board. At present, while he is a member of the board, he is drawing only his salary as director of marketing in the Department of Agriculture. The board set up an advertising program which was being carried on in connection with wheat prior to the time Dean Shaw went to England. These activities were going on when he was there, but not under his direction as director of marketing in the Department of Agriculture. The wheat board is operating under the special act which sets it up. It is operating through the Department of Trade and Commerce, both in Canada and outside.
In regard to the activities of the economics branch in Saskatchewan, I can only say that its main activities there at the present time have to do with the land utilization investigations being made throughout the drought area of Saskatchewan.

Why should there be such
a large item for temporary assistance? I notice that the salaries have increased from $32,625 to $54,360, and temporary assistance has increased by about $4,000. Why should such a large item be carried as temporary assistance?

In this branch, the
same as any other, all employees who are taken on are temporary at first. The fact that we are taking on a number of new employees naturally makes the temporary list rather large.
Are these temporary employees marketing experts?

Not necessarily, in connection with this work. These men are taken on, and even if they are going to be permanent eventually they have to be temporary when appointed. All who are taken on for a short period are temporary.

Are the appointments
made by the civil service commission?
All these appointments are made by the civil service commission.

The minister has referred
to officials travelling to different parts of the globe. Owing to the increase in travelling expenses in connection with this department we might almost say it is becoming a roving department. I believe I am right in saying-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that the estimate for travelling expenses alone for the Department of Agriculture amounts to about $965,000, or an increase of $93,000 over last year. That is over ten per cent of the total estimates. Is it the policy of this government that this shall continue to increase each year? Can we expect an estimate of a million dollars next year for travelling expenses in the one department?

If I remember the
figures correctly, the Department of Agriculture was spending about $11,000,000 back in 1928 or 1929. It is one department that was cut very heavily by the former government, probably more than any other department. Apparently the late government did not consider agriculture of as great importance as the present government does. We have been gradually building the department up; it is not yet back where it was when we left it in 1930.

Building it up by increasing travelling expenses. I notice there appears to be a decrease from the estimates of last year. We must bear in mind that the supple-mentaries are yet to come down, which will no doubt increase this item, which now reaches $965,000 for travelling expenses alone.

I was somewhat surprised to hear the minister make the rather facetious reference he did-I am sure it must have been by way of humour-when he mentioned that the previous administration had not quite as high a regard for agriculture as this administration has. He must have been listening to the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman).
He expressed a general opinion.

I would point out that
there is among farmers in eastern Canada a growing feeling that much more attention should be paid to them and their problems than is paid by this House of Commons. Although we spend in the neighbourhood of half a billion dollars here, only one-fiftieth
of the entire expenditure goes to agriculture. It is not much wonder that the farmers of eastern Canada are asking members of parliament what is being done for eastern Canadian agriculture. Something must be done soon to help many of these specialty lines of agriculture in which eastern Canada is so much interested. I am sure there is not one hon. member from an agricultural constituency in eastern Canada who begrudges the amounts given from time to time to agricultural pursuits in other parts of Canada. And while I have never advocated a rising tide of expenditure, but rather the opposite, I think there are many departments of government which might give way and have their estimates reduced and thereby allow more to be spent upon the development of eastern Canadian agriculture. One particular problem in many ridings similar to my own is in connection with vegetables. Vegetables may not seem so very important to the minister, but I point out to him this cogent fact, that the problem of the vegetable grower in Ontario and elsewhere is one which ultimately must be met.

speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but fruit and vegetables come under the next item, No. 10.

The Minister of Agriculture looks very much interested, and perhaps the committee will allow me to finish my remarks in regard to agricultural economics. I am speaking more particularly on the subject of research. In any event I may point out to the minister that so far as the vegetable growing industry in eastern Canada is concerned there is a feeling that these growers do not always get a square deal. I think some of this money which is voted from time to time for research might well be applied to the vegetable industry in the province of Ontario and elsewhere. Among their other grievances 'the vegetable growers feel that the statistics with regard to their industry, for instance, do not indicate the real importance of that industry to Canada as a whole, and I would suggest to the minister that this is one way in which a substantial portion of the money voted for agricultural economics might very well be spent. I draw that to the attention of the minister in all fairness, and I hope when he has further remarks to make with regard to the contrast as compared with the administration of previous years, he will consider that, after all, in those years conditions generally were somewhat different from the conditions that exist to-day.

Hear, hear.

Supply-Agriculture-Economics

We did not have the expanding revenues of the present day; nor did we have the expanding expenditures, I would point out to the hon. member for Huron-Perth. Having regard to our expenditures throughout Canada as a whole, it seems to me that under this administration the Department of Agriculture has not received a fair proportion of that increased expenditure.

On March 16 'the hon.
member for Essex East introduced a resolution in this house, the latter part of which I should like to read. I shall noit read the preamble, which is a tome in itself, but the latter part states:
Therefore be it resolved,-that, in the opinion of this house, the government
(a)	should consider the necessity for improved marketing facilities;
(b)	should consider the need for providing adequate storage, drying, government grading and inspection facilities in order that the quality of the corn be improved and its production increased.
That motion was agreed to, and I think it would be of interest to the committee if the minister would state what has since been done in this connection.

Before the minister replies, perhaps I, as the mover of that resolution, might be given an opportunity to say a word. When the resolution was brought forward, the Minister of Agriculture was not in his place, and it will be remembered that the Minister of Trade and Commerce accepted the resolution in so far as it dealt with the grading, inspection and weighing of com.
Before the Minister of Agriculture replies,
I may say also that the board of grain commissioners have made arrangements pursuant to the observations of the Minister of Trade and 'Commerce, and will this month, I am advised, visit Canada's outstanding riding, Essex East, which is the greatest county in Canada, to consider and to implement the observations made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I thank the hon. member for Greenwood, who represents a city riding and who has not the opportunity that is afforded me and many other hon, members, to represent so many farmers in this country, for making the .observations he did make, because it will give the Minister of Agriculture a chance to tell the committee first of all that he had the opportunity of reading my speech, and, second, of telling the committee briefly what his department considers to be the importance to this country of the great com growing industry of western Ontario.

One of the few speeches I have read this session was the speech of the hon. member for Essex East in regard to corn. Ever since I came to this house the hon. member has been extremely persistent in placing before the government the requirements of Essex East in relation to corn. We had two different inquiries made in that section before the resolution was moved in the house, and as a result of those inquiries we have improved our methods of assistance in regard to the production of better seed in that area, and the improvement of the seed generally that is being used by farmers in that section of Ontario. In addition, we have adopted a certain policy in connection with the encouragement of the establishment of driers, somewhat on the basis of our policy in connection with cold storage warehouses, which was discussed earlier in the day. As yet no desire has been expressed to have that policy developed in that section, but we hope something along that line may be done during this summer. So far as this department is able to cooperate with the Department of Trade and Commerce in promoting the marketing of corn in those counties, we shall be pleased to do so.
In reply .to the hon. member for Peel, I would say that last summer I had the privilege of driving through Essex East, Kent and other sections where vegetable growing is a very important branch of agriculture. I quite agree with him that very few people outside that section of Canada realize the importance of the vegetable growing industry both to that section and to Canada as a whole. I am sure that when we come to item No. 10, which has to do with fruit and vegetables, the hon. member will be desirous of obtaining further information.

When the Minister of Agriculture says that after going through the county of Essex and adjacent parts of Ontario, his understanding of the great vegetable growing industry was very largely increased, he greatly encourages me. May I suggest that to conclude his investigation, and as the crowning point in the formation of his opinion, he should drop into the county of Peel some time and look it over. Then he will become convinced beyond all shadow of doubt that the vegetable growing industry really amounts to something in this country.

The minister has been very agreeable to-night, and I think the chairman has been quite lenient in allowing such a wide range of discussion. I did want to have something to say about what the minister said
