with regard to the cheese producers' association, and I should have liked to ask further questions about the reorganization. The minister gave us a good deal of information about this reorganization, but if he would prefer that I wait and ask the questions on another item, perhaps when the last item of his department comes up, I am perfectly willing to do so.

I do not want to hold up the item for any length of time, but it seems to me the government might give us some intimation as to what steps have been taken towards greater coordination as between the federal and provincial departments of agriculture. I think this might well come under the agricultural economics branch, since in the last half hour we have discussed so many matters that it would seem that almost anything might come under this branch. I believe some time ago in Ontario it was even suggested by the premier of the province that the provincial departments of agriculture, labour and health might be taken over by the government at Ottawa.
Who made that suggestion?

The
premier of Ontario. Whether or not after that time he lost confidence in this government I do not know, so I cannot say whether that, is still under consideration by the government at Queen's Park. It at least gives rise to concern as to what might be done by way of coordination of effort. I believe it was the intention of those who drew up the British North America Act that the provinces would have to do with the production and the dominion would have to do with the distribution of agricultural products. It was understood, I believe, that the different provinces would establish the departments for that purpose. One can readily see from the reports given to the house that the dominion department has gone far afield from what was considered the original intent under the British North America Act. In these days almost as much consideration is given to production by the dominion department. I am not suggesting for one moment that consideration of production should be confined entirely to the provinces, but I feel that in order to standardize our grades it is necessary that there should be coordination of the efforts of the provinces. The minister has not given us any indication as to what steps, if any, have been taken, or what consideration has been given to a closer coordination of efforts of the different departments. While
travelling expenses have been paid for efficient officers who have travelled far afield to study agricultural economics in other countries, it is my belief that more attention should be given to certain conditions in connection with research which could be carried on in Canada.
According to the minister's report I realize that many matters were considered by this branch. Among other things he has mentioned the utilization of lands in Saskatchewan and Alberta, the consumption of agricultural products in representative cities, a study of the terminal market facilities for fruits and vegetables in the city of Toronto, and an analysis of farm loan experience in Saskatchewan. It would appear that the economics branch deals with the broader interests of Canadian agriculture rather than simply the matter of overseas marketing. I believe the minister would do well to tell us what was done in connection with cooperation with the provinces with respect to local production and distribution, especially in view of the fact that such a high percentage of our market is in Canada.

This whole matter
was discussed under item No. 3, the vote dealing with the advisory committee on agricultural services. That committee is set up, meets at least twice a year and it is discussing these questions continuously. I do not wish to discuss a matter which has been discussed before under the proper item.

The report of last year makes specific reference to the economics branch. Surely the minister would not imply that all these matters are considered under item No. 3 in the estimates where an expenditure of only $5,000 is involved? The matter I have in mind involves an expenditure of $120,000. Surely the item of agricultural economics was not fully discussed under item No. 3?

The economics branch
is concerned only in so far as it may prevent overlapping with economics investigations that are carried on. Those are carried on in cooperation with the provincial governments. It is only on the request and in cooperation with them that these investigations are carried on.

I notice in the details
at page 55 of the estimates with respect to agricultural economics that there is an increase in staff from twelve to twenty, and an additional salary vote from $55,641.25 to $82,520. Would the minister give some information with respect to the extension of services involved?

There is a salaries increase of $26,878.75. Then, under the heading of "permanent," there is provision for eight positions authorized for additional activities in connection with the organization of agricultural marketing services; the promotion and upward revision and classification of rates authorized by the civil service commission, amounting to $1,740. Then, there is provision for statutory increases to the extent of $1,425; return of salary deductions amounting to $1,518.75, and the temporary amount required to pay salary for a full year to the personnel taken on during 1937 and 1938, $2,272. Then, for one stenographer, grade 1, authorized September 16, 1937, there is an amount of $720, and the statutory increase for the office boy, amounting to $240. There is the return of salary reductions amounting to $513, giving a total of $3,745.
Then, for four positions abolished there is the amount of $6,120, and the amount required for additional temporary staff is $6,000. In connection with travelling expenses the increase amounts to $10,123, the break-up showing the expenses of the staff of the markets information division organized in 1937 as amounting to $2,000. There is provision for travelling expenses in connection with the study of the demand for Canadian farm products in the United Kingdom, amounting to $2,250, and a further provision for travelling expenses in Canada in connection with following new projects, the analysis of prices and grades of apples, the study and cost of farm living, the survey of credit in Ontario, the Agricultural Outlook, and special investigations, totalling $5,873. The miscellaneous item amounts to $1,015.

I thank the minister for that information, although I had not expected he would give it in such detail. As I understand the situation, the increase is largely brought about by virtue of increased marketing service activities.
I believe the Agricultural Situation and Outlook, which is published every year, comes under this vote. In vieiw of the avalanche of criticism one hears in connection with votes of this kind, I think we ought, on the other hand to give credit where credit is due. My own personal experience, and I believe that of a great many farmers, has been that the editions of the Agricultural Situation and Outlook have been most useful in connection with agricultural problems. Most of us who came from farms have seen great numbers of agricultural publications of a useless type come through the mail, and we are pleased to 
welcome something as practical as the Agricultural Situation and Outlook has proved to be. I do not think we should let this opportunity pass without expressing our appreciation of the efforts made by those who edit this publication to provide a first class service for the farmers of our country. The farmers in my constituency seem to be more than satisfied with the type of service given by this publication. I do not think there is any other publication issued by the department that is more acceptable to practical farmers.

I have in my hand the report of the Minister of Agriculture for 1937. In that part of it having to do with the economics branch, it states that the research activities of this branch were continued during the year. One of the chief items of research was the consumption of agricultural products in representative cities throughout the dominion. I do not know just how far that investigation has proceeded, but it seems to me that it brings up a live question in connection with the importation of vegetable oils and its effect upon the consumption of lard and butter in our cities. Have the officials who are conducting this investigation made any report to the department? How far has the investigation been continued? I think this is a matter that affects agriculture not only in Ontario but throughout the dominion. Sooner or later we shall have to make a complete study of the effect that these importations have upon the agricultural life of our country, particularly our live stock industry.

Investigations have been carried on in Vancouver, Calgary, Oshawa and Quebec, and the reports thereon are now available to any one who desires to get them. There has been no special investigation into the relationship of vegetable oil importations and the consumption of dairy products. It is well known that last year there was an increase in the production of dairy products as well as in the consumption. Whether there would have been a greater consumption had there not been so much vegetable oil coming in, is something I am not at the moment prepared to say. That is a question upon which there has been considerable discussion.

That is a vague answer. I believe the minister, like some of the rest of us, has a decided idea as to what effect the use of vegetable oils for shortening and spreading purposes has upon our live stock industry, our dairy industry and our fish industry. Is it contemplated that any such investigation shall be held? It seems to me that is one line along which research could

be made. It would prove of great advantage to agriculture generally. The minister named the four cities in which an investigation has been conducted, and without wanting to say anything against any of these cities I think it will be admitted that Oshawa and Quebec are not our larger centres of population. Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg are our largest cities, and it seems to me it would have been more to the point to conduct investigations at those points. I do not know who was responsible for choosing these cities, but surely some investigation should be undertaken along the line I have indicated.

The cities chosen for
the first investigation were typical cities. Provision is being made in this item for a survey of the Ottawa market. I think I stated earlier in the evening that provision is also being made in connection with Toronto. The investigations have been completed in the four cities I have named, but the work is continuing from one end of Canada to the other.
How are the investigations being conducted?
Under Doctor Booth in cooperation with the provincial authorities.
What is the procedure?
A house to house canvass as to consumption.
Will there be an extensive study made of the effect of the importation of vegetable oils upon our dairy industry?
I stated a moment ago that this is not being done.

Will it be included in
the investigations being made?

Not under the present
study.

This is a live question
among householders who are beginning to realize that much of their shortening is made of vegetable oil.

I think
this is very important because of that one factor.
It is not proper for us to discuss it; that is the only thing.

Whenever
the minister is asked a question which he finds it difficult to answer, he says it should be brought up under another item. I suggest that he has a lot more to answer than that question.

Since the hon. gentleman has taken that attitude, I should like to tell him that the item under which this should have been discussed has been passed already. We have passed the item dealing with dairy products, and that was the one under which this matter should have been discussed. If it is simply a case of carrying over this item to another day because the hon. member did not avail himself of the opportunity of asking his question under that item, then I should like to say that we shall have to stay closer to the rules in future discussions.

I do not
want the minister to assume now that I am taking any particular attitude.
Progress reported.
